summary: Describes management and operational requirements for the address and routing parameter area domain, arpa, which is a special part of the DNS. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: The arpa domain holds special DNS names used by Internet infrastructure, including reverse address lookups. RFC 3172 explains who manages it and how new parts can be added.

subtitle: The management rules for arpa, a DNS domain reserved for Internet infrastructure identifiers.

tldr.problem: The arpa domain supports reverse lookups and other infrastructure data used by Internet services. Its administration must be stable and controlled.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB manages arpa with ICANN, while IANA carries out its administration. New sub-domains need an IETF Standards Track specification that recommends arpa and describes the delegation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3172 is a Best Current Practice. The unit metadata says RFC 9120 updates it.

facts.label: Root server requirements
facts.value: RFC 2870 requirements also apply to arpa servers

today: RFC 3172 is a Best Current Practice and is updated by RFC 9120. Read that update alongside this document.

sections.title: Why the arpa Domain Matters
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) usually maps names to protocol values, such as domain names to IP addresses. DNS can also map protocol values back to service names by turning them into names that can be looked up.

For example, an IPv4 address can be turned into a name under in-addr.arpa, where a DNS record can point to a domain name. Applications rely on the correct operation of arpa name servers.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS can look up a name from an address as well as an address from a name. The arpa domain provides the special names used for some of these reverse lookups.

sections.title: arpa Is an Infrastructure Domain
sections.content:
The arpa domain began as part of the early DNS deployment and provided a home for IPv4 reverse mapping. In 2000 its name was expanded as “Address and Routing Parameter Area.”

It is an infrastructure domain: it supports Internet operations and is not intended for ordinary host naming. IANA performs its operational administration under the arrangement described by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: arpa is reserved for names that support Internet operations. It is not a general-purpose place to register ordinary computer names.

sections.title: Who Manages arpa
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB), working with ICANN, is responsible for managing the arpa top-level domain. IANA performs operational administration under the agreement between the IAB and ICANN.

The IAB decides what protocol information belongs in arpa and how its name structure is organized. It may delegate management of a sub-domain to an appropriate protocol management group.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB decides what belongs in arpa, working with ICANN. IANA handles its day-to-day administration, and management of a sub-domain can be delegated.

sections.title: How New Sub-domains Are Approved
sections.content:
The IAB should recommend a new arpa sub-domain only when an IETF Standards Track document describes the delegation and name structure and explicitly recommends using arpa in its IANA Considerations.

That section should name the sub-domain, explain its administration, and set entry criteria. The IESG reviews the proposal; if it approves the document, it asks the IAB to request the delegation from IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: A new arpa sub-domain needs a published IETF standard that explains its purpose and rules. The IESG reviews the proposal before the IAB asks IANA to create it.

sections.title: Name Server and Security Requirements
sections.content:
arpa sits directly below the DNS root so that locating its servers does not require several lookups across separate operational domains. The RFC applies the root name server operational requirements in RFC 2870 to arpa servers.

Any new sub-domain delegation must document security issues specific to the information it stores. Security rules in RFC 2870 and later successors also apply to arpa server operation.
sections.plainLanguage: arpa servers follow the operational requirements for root servers. A proposal for a new sub-domain must also explain security issues tied to its data.

sections.title: Sub-domains Listed in the RFC
sections.content:
RFC 3172 lists in-addr.arpa for IPv4 reverse mapping, ip6.arpa for IPv6 reverse mapping, and e164.arpa for mapping telephone numbers into URIs.

The RFC describes the arrangements and plans at the time it was written, including work to move arpa records off some root servers. These descriptions are historical context, not claims about present-day operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names three arpa sub-domains: one for IPv4 reverse lookups, one for IPv6 reverse lookups, and one for telephone-number lookups. It describes their arrangements as they stood when the document was written.
